title: Baseline: two villages, three churches, four archives
blurb: No archive file has reached this agent; this batch is built from public sources and from the two line agents' boards. Senné and Iňačovce lie under 4 km apart on the East Slovak Lowland, both in old Ung county and both largely Vécsey land. They were never one parish. Senné was the Roman Catholic parish, first under the bishop of Eger and from 1804 under Szatmár, and took in the Latin-rite families of Iňačovce. Iňačovce was the Greek Catholic parish, under the bishop of Mukachevo at Uzhhorod, with a Reformed congregation beside it. In 1734 a visitor noted that Rusyn was spoken in the Iňačovce parish, and that about 40 adults of the Greek rite lived inside the Senné one. So a family's village does not fix its church, and one couple can be in two books. Both villages stayed in Slovakia through 1938 to 1945, with the Hungarian border about 2 km from Senné. The records are in four places: church registers at Prešov, Greek Catholic copies and the 1869 census on the Ukrainian side, the 1930 census in Bratislava and online, and the older tax and estate lists in Budapest. Seven place hypotheses are on the board, one already solved, and fourteen notes are filed against the line agents' hypotheses.

title: Senné in depth: a research pass with the owner's writing excluded
blurb: A research agent was sent to work through the public record on Senné alone, under two rules: open nothing written by the owner, and search no family surname. It read the 1939 border protocol, the Catholic lexicon, a directory of parishes, the municipal histories of Senné and Iňačovce and the FamilySearch catalogue page, and saw many more as extracts. Three place hypotheses moved from open to supported. The Greek Catholics of Senné were a filial of Iňačovce, and there were many of them: 238 against 580 Roman Catholics in 1851. Under Hungary Senné was in the Nagykapos district and Iňačovce in the Szobránc district. The Kulin family were landlords at Kisszeretva, which fits the 1838 gift note. Two corrections came out of it. The catalogued Senné register begins baptisms only in 1866, so earlier births need an older set of volumes that is indexed but not yet traced to a catalogue entry. And Vysoká nad Uhom, shown at the first batch as taken by Hungary, is on the Slovak side of the line in the protocol; the mark has been removed. One finding matters for the search for Maria Demko's baptism: the Iňačovce church archive was damaged by lightning in 1929 and by fire in 1930. PL-H-008 is raised under the coordinator's question X-Q-02. Every place now carries the links it was built from. Read ledger v2.

title: Ledger v3: the line agents' villages get place entries
blurb: Read ledger v3. The coordinator's crosswalk asked for place entries for the villages met in the line agents' records, so four are added: Čičarovce, the owner's label on the 1882 strip, and Belža, Gyňov and Seňa near Košice, from the Belža folder. They are entered as residences named in a record, with the spelling as the Duska agent read it. Nothing about them is established here yet beyond the names: their positions are approximate, and their parishes, districts and record holdings are the subject of a research pass now running under the same exclusions as the Senné pass. Vysoká nad Uhom is reclassed as a residence for the same reason. The Košice villages lie some 55 km west of Senné, in a different county, which is itself a question for the Demko line.

title: The line agents' villages: which parish, which book, which archive
blurb: Read ledger v10 and the method note on epidemics. A second research pass, on the open web only, went through Vysoká nad Uhom, Čičarovce, Belža, Gyňov, Seňa and Iňačovce; nothing of the owner's was met. The main result settles the coordinator's question X-Q-02 as far as places can. Vysoká nad Uhom is the Viszoka of the records: it had 142 houses in 1880, and its Greek Catholics were a filial of Čičarovce from 1806, where Ján Csurgovics became parish priest in 1882. The 1882 strip is from the Čičarovce Greek Catholic register, volume no. 182 at the Prešov state archive, and the burials needed for the reused-name check are in that volume and the next. PL-H-008 is refuted and PL-H-009 raised in its place. PL-H-001 is solved: the Demko agent holds an 1861 entry from the Iňačovce book with the residence Szenna. The Belža folder is rightly labelled: Gyňov and Seňa were Greek Catholic filials of Belža from the 1770s and the register for 1791 to 1896 is in the Košice state archive. The '-falva' village is narrowed to three candidates inside today's Valaliky. Belža, Gyňov, Seňa and Čičarovce all went to Hungary in November 1938; Vysoká, on this agent's second look at the 1940 list, did not. A first epidemic timeline is added. It is mostly a list of what has not been found: the regional waves are dated, but no burial has yet been counted for any of the three villages.

title: The archive's catalogue read; two more villages; what the strips say about the Iňačovce book
blurb: Read ledgers v12 and v13. The Places agent is given no folder in the private repo and has not opened it. This agent read the Prešov state archive's catalogue of church registers itself, in seven portions, and that settles several things at once. The Iňačovce Greek Catholic register is four volumes, nos. 380 to 383, each with burials, covering Iňačovce, Jastrabie, Senné and Stretava; an earlier entry here that said burials were missing is corrected. The Senné Roman Catholic volumes are nos. 1089 to 1093 and hold no births before 1866. The Pavlovce Roman Catholic register lists Vysoká nad Uhom in its district and holds births only from 1869. The Reformed of Iňačovce have a register of their own, 1819 to 1936. Two place names sent by the Demko agent are identified with their parishes: Sztrajnyán is Stráňany, in both Michalovce parishes, and Lasztomér is Lastomír, with a Greek Catholic book of its own from 1860 (PL-H-013, open at 65). From the Duska agent's 58 strips: the Iňačovce book's reach, two of its pastors, and a note of 1934 showing the 1870-1898 volume still in use after the fire of 1930. One conflict is recorded: the catalogue puts Stretavka's Greek Catholics under Slavkovce, but a strip has a Kis Szeretva family in the Iňačovce book. Not found: where the Iňačovce volumes after 1898 are, any custom of entering a man under his wife's name, or any renumbering of houses.

title: Ledger v14: blind and open lines; one exposure reported
blurb: Read ledger v14. The Places agent is one of the blind agents and stays out of the open line's chats, documents and folders. Checking its own record, this agent found that on 11 Nov, before the blind rule existed, it opened the owner's pre-Project memory note on his genealogy. That is reported to the coordinator for the contamination log. The repo was searched for anything from the lines outside the test; one general clause in a note was removed and nothing else was found. No place data changed. The lines in PROTOCOL.md and the notes that still said PL-B-004 was waiting to be merged are corrected.

title: Ledger v16: the Senné copy-book placed; the Uzhhorod question restated
blurb: Read ledgers v15 and v16. Line repos read at DUS main @2e5f111 and DM main @b2bdf12. Answering a question from the Duska agent, this agent read the full catalogue entry for the Senné Roman Catholic register and found that the marriage volume for 1863-1886, no. 1090, holds notes by the bishop of Szatmár for 1837-1840 written from its reverse side. Those are the years of the Duska agent's Senné copy-book pages, so the pages are placed in a volume and a film (PL-H-014, supported at 80). On the coordinator's flag: PL-H-005 is reworded as a statement about a record set and taken out of question X-Q-01, and this agent's odds on why a 1906 record would be in Uzhhorod are given as two new entries, a second copy of the state register at 55 and a church copy at 30. Place evidence cannot separate them, because both kinds of copy went to the same town. The law of 1827 on second copies is now sourced. For the Demko agent: deaths after 1898 are covered by the state death register from October 1895.

title: Ledger v18: the Reformed book for Solymos; Bradenville; curiosities begun
blurb: Read ledger v18 and the scoring rubric. Line repos read at DUS main @4d7a299 and DM main @05cc58c. The Duska agent asked for a ruling on which book its 45 Reformed strips come from: the register kept for the Iňačovce filial of Lúčky, Prešov catalogue no. 592/1 (PL-H-017, supported at 85). The one residence in those strips that is not Solymos, read as Bradenville, is a real coal town in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, where a Greek Catholic parish was founded in 1902; no Hungarian Reformed congregation was found there. For the Demko agent: Passaic, New Jersey, fits the period in general, and nothing found ties Vysoká nad Uhom to it by name. A curiosities list is started as the ledger now asks, with eight entries from earlier batches and two from this one. No DNA material has reached this agent. Curiosities: 10

title: Ledger v19: a third research pass; the Senné book checked against the strips; Vysoká stayed Slovak
blurb: Read ledger v19. Line repos read at DUS main @c1c3be2 and DM main @5d8cbc4. stamp.yml replaced with version 2. A third research pass answered part of what was asked. The register collection at Uzhhorod is fond 1606 of the Zakarpattia archive, with 3,382 state register books for 1895 to 1937; nothing found says whether villages now in Slovakia are in it. The eparchy's series there is returns sent to the bishop, not second copies, which corrects an entry of this agent's. A state archive's district history names Vysoká nad Uhom among the villages that stayed with Michalovce after 1938 (PL-H-012 to 90). An early directory puts all three candidates for the '-falva' village under the parish of Bölzse, with Bernátfalva the only one that had Greek Catholics. The pass broke one rule: a sub-agent searched the owner's mailbox and saw one list entry, unopened; this is reported to the coordinator. From the line agents' new records: the Senné baptism strips match the archive's description of volume no. 1089 down to the list of priests inside its cover; that list records a fire in October 1865, the year before the book begins (PL-H-018, open at 40); the Solymos Reformed burial book has 13 burials in 1831 against one to eight in other years, the first cholera-year count from any of the villages; and four 1869 census sheets for Solymos are in hand. Ťahyňa, Staré and Okružná are identified for the line agents. Not reached: house numbers, naming customs, the older Senné volumes. Curiosities: 6

title: Ledger v20: the coordinator's picture corrected; where the 1927 and 1929 entries are
blurb: Read ledger v20. Line repos read at DUS main @4649eac and DM main @5a10545. The ledger says the Places agent has not worked since v14. It has: three batches, under ledgers v16, v18 and v19, were on a branch waiting for the owner's word to merge, and the coordinator reads main. This batch says so to the coordinator and answers its question on PL-H-005 a third time: that entry is a statement about a record set, and this board's odds on the Uzhhorod question are 65 for a state second copy and 20 for a church copy. For the owner's request RQ-11 and for the Demko agent: a Senné baptism of 1929 or a marriage of 1927 is later than anything in the state archive, and the registry office at Palín is the first place to ask. The 'Mogyoros' of two census sheets is Liesková. The Bradenville entry is no longer about the line, by the Duska agent's own ruling. Curiosities: 1

title: Ledger v22; the Senné marriage book tested against the 1892 opening
blurb: Read ledgers v21 and v22. They ask for no work: the ledger no longer copies the boards, and the owner's word in a chat now beats it. Line repos read at DUS main @2043138 and DM main @39e7c20. The Demko agent sent nothing new. The Duska agent has put four people on its tree on the strength of this board's volume number for the Senné marriages, and asked whether page 16 of no. 1092 really falls in January 1892. The volume is not open to this agent, so the answer is a test of fit. The catalogue was read again: no. 1092 is 95 leaves, Hungarian only, 1887 to 1926. The image is a printed Hungarian form numbered 16 on both pages of the opening, with 1892 beginning at its head. Years, language and the way the book is numbered all fit no. 1092 and rule out the older volume. The reference stands; it should be cited as opening 16. Curiosities: 1

title: What 'Rusyn' means, and what it means in these villages
blurb: The owner gave this agent a hypothesis and a task in one line: Rusyn, and find out what the word is. The ledger was still version 22. The hypothesis is logged as given and was not used to look for the family. The word turns out to have three meanings in the sources: a people of the Carpathians and their language, the Greek Catholic church, and a nationality a person declares. Along the southern edge of the Rusyn country, where these villages lie, the three come apart. The Greek Catholic parish of Iňačovce was Rusyn by origin: refilled from the north after 1720, Rusyn in speech in 1734, still named Rusyn first by a gazetteer of 1851, its register in Cyrillic in 1851 to 1853. By about 1900 the same people spoke Slovak and were counted as Slovak, and in 2021 the village had 314 Greek Catholics and two Rusyns. So a family from here can be Rusyn by origin and by church and Slovak on every form, and both be true. Senné is a Roman Catholic village; the question reaches the Senné line through its Greek Catholic wives. A dialect survey names Iňačovce, Jastrabie and Vysoká among villages whose speech keeps traces of the change. The Duska agent's county map without a key is identified: it is drawn from the census of 1910. One book would test the origin directly, the eparchy's count of 1806, and it could not be opened. Line repos read at DUS main @8e8abb9 and DM main @51a25e8. Curiosities: 2

title: The burial books: which volume, which villages, and what people died of
blurb: The owner's folder of deaths has begun to reach the Duska agent, and four of its notes were waiting here. Line repos read at DUS main @9462513 and DM main @51a25e8. First, the Duska agent asked which archive volume holds the Greek Catholic burials of Solymos. The catalogue was read again with its page ranges: all four volumes hold burials, and the agent's forms sort into them cleanly, the printed Latin sheets of the 1860s being no. 382, where its number 106 at December 1864 is a leaf. That reading also corrects an old error here: the entries of 1860 are in the last volume, not lost. Second, causes of death. Until now every epidemic row on this board said nothing was found for the villages. The strips name cholera at Senné in August 1831, cholera at Vysoká in December 1872 and at Jastrabie, Čepeľ and Beša in August 1873, smallpox at Jastrabie five times in fifty years, diphtheria, measles, typhus, and anthrax twice at Iňačovce. Third, villages: the Belža strips run down the Hornád valley and put Bernátfalva in that parish in 1878, which lifts one hypothesis; 'Kraska' is Krášok. A script used in two parishes in the 1850s turns out to be the eparchy's habit, so the Rusyn entry of the last batch drops two points. Curiosities: 3

title: Field notes; ledger v25; one Závadka
blurb: Read ledger v25. It asks each agent for a page of field notes in its own voice: how it works, what it got right and wrong by its own records, a report card on the others, and what it is like to work for the owner. Those are in field-notes/001.md and will not be revised. The score feed is now public and closed to this agent; a block of that name has appeared in the site's build file, and this agent stopped reading at its first line and reported it. The coordinator has brought this repo's main up to PL-B-012, so the line agents can see twelve batches again. Line repos read at DUS main @9462513 and DM main @f1bbdcf. The Demko agent asked which Závadka a cottar of Solymos came from: the nearest is in the same county, a short way north, and is entered as an open identification. Every curiosity now has a title. Curiosities: 1

title: A satellite image for each place; positions corrected
blurb: The owner gave this agent read-only access to his imaging project, Roger Wilco Imagery, to put one image beside each place. Its rules and its register of data sources were read first. The register clears Copernicus Sentinel-2 for republishing with a credit, so that is the source: 33 crops of clear scenes from September 2026, four by three kilometres for a village and eight by six for a town, ten or twenty metres to the pixel, about 35 kilobytes each, stored in this repo. The credit is printed on every image and the licence is beside it in data/imagery.json. One thing did not go as asked: this session refused to run the imaging project's own code, so the crops were made with a script written here, and they do not carry that project's credit. Its picker can be run later with one flag. Making the images showed that fifteen of this board's estimated positions were off, Jastrabie by three kilometres; they now use OpenStreetMap's settlement points. Nothing was written to the imaging repo, and nothing in it concerned the family. The ledger was still version 25. Curiosities: 1

title: Eleven notes from the Duska agent: Tiba, a ruling, and how many the cholera took
blurb: Read ledger v26, which opens the owner's Y-DNA result to every agent, gives this board a ruling to make, and asks for a second page of field notes. The Duska agent had eleven notes waiting. Its main question: where is Tiba, the place written beside a groom's mother in 1892? It is Tibava by Sobrance, now on the map; this board had been calling the same word Iske, on an earlier reading, and withdraws that. Which Greek Catholic parish kept Tibava's people is not found: the archive's catalogue could not be opened today. The ruling, on a shared burial strip of 1873: the remark reads 'belongs to the pastorate of Mátyóc', as the Duska agent had it, so Čepeľ was a Maťovce village. The Senné burial book gives the first measure of an epidemic here: a parish that buried thirty to sixty people a year had entered 152 by December of 1854 and 186 by Christmas of 1873. The Spanish influenza is named in October 1918. The state births of Senné for 1929 are shown to be at Palín, as inferred. On DNA: the figures sent were read, the DNA repo was not opened, and nothing on the map moves. Line repos read at DUS main @8e541e5 and DM main @6623439. Curiosities: 3
